results.summary: This project implements a bandgap voltage reference in the SkyWater 130nm process, producing an approximately 0.9V analog output on ua[0]. The design is written in Verilog but is an analog macro, with all digital inputs unused. It requires external measurement equipment to verify the reference voltage. The documentation is minimal, providing only the output voltage and pin assignment, so little else can be said about its implementation or performance.

This design implements a complete Blackjack card game in Verilog for a 1x1 Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a finite state machine to manage game flow, an LFSR for card randomness, and outputs game status via LEDs and a 3-bit sum to a 7-segment display. The game is controlled by hit and stand buttons, with win/lose/push indicated by LEDs. External hardware needed includes a clock source, push buttons, LEDs, and a 7-segment display; button debouncing is optional.

This project is a generative art piece that creates recursive rectangle patterns, described as 'silicon cross stitch', on a 2x2 tile canvas. It is written in Verilog and has a single dummy output pin, with no inputs or control interface. The design is purely visual and requires no external hardware; it is meant to be observed rather than tested. The documentation is very sparse, offering only a brief description and no technical details.

This design combines a Bernoulli stochastic multiplier, a conventional 4x4 unsigned multiplier, and a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron on a single tile. The stochastic multiplier uses two LFSRs to generate random thresholds and estimates the product of two 4-bit probabilities over a window of cycles, while the conventional multiplier provides an exact product for comparison. The LIF neuron is a signed 8-bit integer model with configurable threshold, reset, and decay, and outputs a spike and membrane potential. The design is selected via two project select pins and requires no external hardware.

This design generates a VGA output showing a pseudo-3D sine wave ribbon animation and also produces simple music via an audio output pin. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock and external VGA and audio PMODs to view and hear the output. The documentation is incomplete, with a TODO note, but the pinout matches the Tiny VGA and TT Audio standards. The project is a light-hearted demo, as indicated by its description.

This project is a low-dropout (LDO) linear regulator implemented in an analog process, capable of supplying 0.1 to 4 mA at an output voltage of 1.4 to 1.8V. It consists of a BJT bandgap reference, two op-amps, and a pass PMOS transistor, with an external reference current set by a 90k resistor. The output voltage is available on ua[0], and testing requires a multimeter. The documentation is brief but provides the essential information for basic operation.

This design is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It uses a legacy layout bit cell, which is larger than a thin-cell version, and is kept for historical reasons. The SRAM operates on a 66 MHz clock, with read and write operations controlled by a write-enable signal, and write-through behavior. Testing involves performing read and write operations and verifying data retention.

This design is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins, using the same SRAM block as TTSKY-SPSRAM-direct but with pin connections made via librelane. It operates on a 66 MHz clock and supports read and write operations with write-through behavior. The design is intended for use as a standalone SRAM block, and testing involves verifying read and write functionality. The use of librelane for pin connection is notable.

This project is a VGA-based checkers game with modified layer movements and colors, based on a VGA playground design. It outputs VGA signals on the standard Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 25.175 MHz clock. The design is meant to be viewed on a VGA monitor, and no external hardware beyond a VGA connection is specified. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text for external hardware, so details of gameplay or implementation are limited.

This design implements a 127-stage coarse-tapped all-digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL) targeting 125 MHz in the SkyWater 130nm process. It features a structural digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) built from a 127-stage ring oscillator with coarse frequency tapping to switch between full and shortened loops. The feedback loop uses a synchronous digital divider, and the design includes pins for reference clock selection, reset, tap selection, and division ratio configuration. Testing involves applying reset, selecting the reference clock, configuring the tap and division settings, and monitoring the output clock and raw DCO clock.
